title: People who cannot manage their thirst. Part 1
scripture_text: ‘’The Pharisees heard the crowd whispering such things about him. Then the Chief Priests and the Pharisees sent temple guards to arrest him. Jesus said “I am with you for only a short time and then I am going to the one who sent me. You will look for me, but you will not find me; and where I am, you cannot come.” The Jews said to one another, “Where does this man intend to go that we cannot find him? Will he go where our people live scattered among the Greeks, and teach the Greeks? What did he mean when he said, ‘You will look for me, but you will not find me,’ and ‘Where I am, you cannot come’?”
devotional:
On the last and greatest day of the festival, Jesus stood and said in a loud voice, “Let anyone who is thirsty come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as Scripture has said, rivers of living water will flow from within them.” By this he meant the Spirit whom those who believed in him were later to receive. Up to that time the Spirit had not been given, since Jesus had not yet been glorified. On hearing his words, some of the people said, “Surely this man is the Prophet.” Others said, “He is the Messiah.” Still others asked, “How can the Messiah come from Galilee? Does not Scripture say that the Messiah will come from David’s descendants and from Bethlehem the town where David lived?” Thus the people were divided because of Jesus. Some wanted to seize him, but no one laid a hand on him. Finally the temple guards went back to the chief priests and the Pharisees, who asked them, “Why didn’t you bring him in?” “No one ever spoke the way this man does,” the guards replied. “You mean he has deceived you also?” the Pharisees retorted.“Have any of the rulers or of the Pharisees believed in him? No! But this mob that knows nothing of the law—there is a curse on them.”

“Driving up from Beersheba, a combined force of British, Australians and New Zealanders were pressing on the rear of the Turkish retreat over arid desert. The attack outdistanced its water carrying camel train. Water bottles were empty. The sun blazed pitilessly out of a sky where the vultures wheeled expectantly. “Our heads ached,” writes Gilbert, “and our eyes became bloodshot and dim in the blinding glare...Our tongues began to swell...Our lips turned a purplish black and burst. Those who dropped out of the column were never seen again, but the desperate force battled on to Sheria. There were wells at Sheria, and had they been unable to take the place by nightfall, thousands were doomed to die of thirst. “We fought that day,” writes Gilbert, “as men fight for their lives... We entered Sheria station on the heels of the retreating Turks. The first objects which met our view were the great stone cisterns full of cold, clear, drinking water. In the still night air the sound of water running into the tanks could be distinctly heard, maddening in its nearness; yet not a man murmured when orders were given for the battalions to fall in, two deep, facing the cisterns” He then describes the stern priorities: the wounded, those on guard duty, then company by company. It took four hours before the last man had his drink of water, and in all that time they had been standing twenty feet from a low stone wall on the other side of which were thousands of gallons of water.’’ From an account of the British liberation of Palestine by Major V. Gilbert in The Last Crusade, quoted in Christ’s Call To Discipleship, J. M. Boice, Moody, 1986, p143.

Thirst is a powerful thing.

We all know how it feels. We’re hot, dehydrated, with a dry mouth, a sore head and an inability to think about anything except…water, water…

It’s such an ordinary, tasteless, drink and yet it can be hard to want anything more, to desire anything as intensely as that ice-cold glass of pure, clear, water.

There’s nothing like having a thirst quenched. It’s so satisfying. It’s such a sense of relief. It refreshes and restores like nothing else.

It’s no surprise that we talk about ‘thirst’ in relation to lots of other things. It conveys a powerful sense of yearning, needing and searching for something to satisfy.

We all thirst for something. We can all identify with the experience of longing and hoping for something more, something that is real, something that will help us to feel valued and significant. But in reality, thirst is a very difficult thing to manage.

Thirst is an expression of our deepest need but often, we struggle to identify what we are really thirsty for. Even when we think we have recognised what we’re lacking, it’s really easy to turn to inappropriate ways or use inappropriate resources in an attempt to quench our thirst.

Over the next few days, in this next part of the Feast of Tabernacles, we are going to discover some of the wrong ways in which the religious leaders of the time tried to manage their thirst. We’ll see how their inappropriate reactions to Jesus was, in fact, an indicator that they were unable to control or satisfy the thirst that robbed them of real life.

In a desperate attempt to satisfy their thirst for control and their desire to silence Jesus, the insecurity and the hostility of the Pharisees rapidity increases.

Ask yourself ‘What am I thirsty for?’ ‘What do the deepest longings of my heart say about me?’
prayer: Father may I be motivated by the right ‘thirst’s’, help me to honestly identify my thirst.
